# Paths that must NOT be downloadable from the live site.
#
# The check fails if any of these returns HTTP 200. A 403 (blocked) is what we
# want. A 404 also passes, because there is nothing there to leak.
#
# To add a path: put it on its own line, starting with a slash. That's it --
# no YAML, no quoting. Lines starting with # are comments. Trailing comments on
# the same line as a path are NOT supported; put the comment on its own line.

# --- Grav's own bait files. It plants these to test itself, and leaves them ---
/tmp/grav-security-probe.txt
/tmp/grav-security-probe.dat
/tmp/grav-security-probe.zip
/tmp/grav-security-probe.json
/backup/grav-security-probe.zip

# --- Site config and credentials ---
/user/config/system.yaml
/user/config/security.yaml

# --- Logs ---
/logs/grav.log

# --- Hidden files at the web root. .htaccess is always present, so it is a ---
# --- reliable canary for the hidden-file and root-file rules ---
/.htaccess
/.user.ini
/.env.example
/.migration-complete

# --- Dependency inventory. Exposing these hands over the exact version of ---
# --- every library we run, which is how someone shops for a known CVE ---
/vendor/composer/installed.json
/composer.lock
/user/themes/quark/package.json

# --- Sample server configs Grav ships. Harmless alone, but they reveal the ---
# --- stack and they are not ours to serve ---
/webserver-configs/Caddyfile
/webserver-configs/nginx.conf

# --- Page source. Visitors get the rendered page, never the raw markdown ---
/user/pages/02.about-us/17.HISTORY/21._frc-2019/text.md

# --- Version disclosure: names the exact Grav release and its patched CVEs ---
/CHANGELOG.md
